questions.q: Write the molecular formula of the alkane, alkene, and alkyne that each contain exactly three carbon atoms.
questions.a: Alkane (3 C): C₃H₈ (using CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ → 2×3+2=8 H). Alkene (3 C): C₃H₆ (using CₙH₂ₙ → 2×3=6 H). Alkyne (3 C): C₃H₄ (using CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ → 2×3−2=4 H). A wrong answer (e.g., C₃H₆ for alkane) reveals the student has memorised formulas without understanding how valency determines the hydrogen count.

questions.q: Explain why ethene (C₂H₄) is unsaturated while ethane (C₂H₆) is saturated, referring to the type of carbon‑carbon bond and the number of hydrogen atoms attached.
questions.a: Ethene has a carbon‑carbon double bond (C=C); each carbon is bonded to only two hydrogens, so the molecule has fewer hydrogens than the maximum possible for two carbons (which would be 6). Ethane has a carbon‑carbon single bond (C‑C); each carbon carries three hydrogens, giving the maximum hydrogen count (C₂H₆). A student who says “ethene has fewer carbons” or “ethane has more hydrogens because it’s heavier” confuses molecular mass with saturation — the key is bond order, not mass.

questions.q: A hydrocarbon has the molecular formula C₅H₁₀. Identify its class (alkane/alkene/alkyne) and draw one possible structural formula showing all bonds.
questions.a: General formula check: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ for n=5 → C₅H₁₂ (alkane); CₙH₂ₙ → C₅H₁₀ (alkene); CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ → C₅H₈ (alkyne). C₅H₁₀ matches alkene. One structural formula: CH₃‑CH₂‑CH₂‑CH=CH₂ (pent‑1‑ene). A wrong classification (e.g., calling it an alkane) shows the student cannot apply general formulas to a given molecular formula.

questions.q: Compare the hydrogen‑to‑carbon ratio (H/C) in methane (CH₄), ethene (C₂H₄), and ethyne (C₂H₂). What trend do you observe as unsaturation increases?
questions.a: Methane H/C = 4/1 = 4; ethene H/C = 4/2 = 2; ethyne H/C = 2/2 = 1. As unsaturation increases (single → double → triple bond), the H/C ratio decreases because each additional π‑bond reduces the number of hydrogens by two. A student who calculates ratios incorrectly (e.g., 4, 4, 2) or states “ratio increases” has not linked bond multiplicity to hydrogen deficiency.

questions.q: A student writes the structural formula of propyne as CH₃‑C≡C‑H. Is this correct? Justify your answer by counting bonds on each carbon.
questions.a: Yes, it is correct. Left carbon (CH₃): three C‑H bonds + one C‑C bond = 4 bonds. Middle carbon: one C‑C bond + one C≡C triple bond (counts as three bonds) = 4 bonds. Right carbon (C‑H): one C‑H bond + triple bond (three bonds) = 4 bonds. All carbons satisfy tetravalency. A student who says “no, because the middle carbon has only two bonds” is counting the triple bond as one bond instead of three — a common error in bond‑order counting.

questions.q: Design a simple test using bromine water to distinguish between a sample of hexane (C₆H₁₄) and hex‑1‑ene (C₆H₁₂). Describe the observation and the chemical reason.
questions.a: Add bromine water (orange‑brown) to each sample in separate test tubes. Hexane (alkane) shows no colour change — bromine water remains orange because alkanes do not react with bromine at room temperature without UV light. Hex‑1‑ene (alkene) decolourises bromine water immediately due to addition across the C=C bond forming a dibromoalkane. A poor answer that says “both decolourise” or “hexane reacts faster” confuses substitution (needs UV) with addition (occurs readily at room temperature).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ are organic compounds composed exclusively of carbon and hydrogen atoms.

Fill in the blank: ______ a kitchen LPG cylinder (mostly butane, an alkane), a candle flame (paraffin wax = long‑chain alkanes), a fruit‑ripening pouch (releases ethene, an alkene), and a welder’s torch (uses ethyne/acetylene, an alkyne).
What is Hydrocarbons? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Hydrocarbons are organic compounds composed exclusively of carbon and hydrogen atoms.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Hydrocarbons?
questions.a: Students often think that “unsaturated” means the molecule has “empty space” or “can hold more hydrogen” in a vague sense, and they write the general formula of alkene as CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (same as alkane) because they forget that each double bond reduces the hydrogen count by two relative to the saturated formula.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can (1) write the molecular formula of any alkane, alkene, or alkyne given the number of carbon atoms, (2) draw the structural formula (showing all bonds) for the first four members of each series, and (3) distinguish saturated from unsaturated hydrocarbons by comparing their general formulas and bond types.
